Area.evidence_source: [/page/11/Text/5] The aim of this qualitative study was to examine individual experiences of spirituality and/or religion in a sample of veterans recognized as being at increased risk of suicide. [/page/11/Text/6] issues related to spirituality and/or religion figured prominently in the lives of these veterans and specifically in their struggles with suicide ideation and attempts. [...] Spirituality/religiosity plays adaptive and maladatpive roles for patients in terms of evaluating suicide as a possible action, understanding and coping with suffering, as well as recovery from a suicide attempt. [/page/11/Text/7] spiritual and/or religious beliefs, practices, and experiences that add to suffering may potentially lower the threshold for suicidal behavior. [...] Conversely, spiritual and/or religious beliefs that [/page/12/Text/1] supported making meaning of suffering included the belief that God has purpose in suffering, ability to separate suffering from enjoyable aspects of life, and finding purpose in suffering. [/page/12/Text/2] both of these veterans described these interventions as vital to their ongoing management of suicidal ideation. The findings presented here suggest that considering spiritual and/or religious experiences in the therapeutic regimen may be a useful component in mitigating suicide risk. [...] facilitating mental health recovery. [/page/12/Text/3] Finally, 12 of the 20 veterans with a history of a suicide attempt attributed their survival to spirituality and/or religion. This included viewing their survival as evidence of Divine intervention, proof that their life had purpose, or uncovering other facets of spiritual significance.
